report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that prolonged use of cloth or surgical masks causes dangerous carbon-dioxide (CO2) buildup is not supported by the weight of scientific evidence. Multiple studies and fact-checks conclude that, for the general public and most healthy individuals, mask-wearing does not cause clinically significant hypercapnia (excess CO2 in the blood).

**Key evidence:**

- A study in *BMC Infectious Diseases* measured CO2 under various masks and found levels rose slightly but remained below dangerous thresholds, even during prolonged use in healthcare workers (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12879-021-06056-0).
- A randomized crossover study of healthy adults found that surgical and N95 masks did not significantly impair oxygen saturation or CO2 levels at rest; changes during exercise stayed within normal physiological limits (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7904135/).
- The CDC and WHO state that properly worn medical masks do not cause CO2 intoxication or oxygen deficiency, because CO2 molecules are small enough to pass through mask materials (https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2021/nov/01/facebook-posts/no-evidence-masks-cause-dangerous-carbon-dioxide-b/).
- Fact-checking organizations (USA Today, Reuters, AFP, Full Fact) consistently found no credible evidence that cloth or surgical masks expose wearers—including children—to dangerous CO2 concentrations, noting that masks are not airtight and allow gas exchange (https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/05/30/fact-check-wearing-face-mask-not-cause-hypoxia-hypercapnia/5260106002/).

**Caveats:** Some studies report minor, transient CO2 increases, especially with N95/FFP2 masks during heavy exertion or in people with severe respiratory disease. However, these changes are generally within safe limits and do not constitute dangerous buildup for the general population.
